evidence.quote: This Byway begins twelve miles north of Carlsbad in the Chihuahuan Desert and ascends about 3,000 feet into the Guadalupe Mountains.

evidence.claim: NM 137’s approach changed during the Brantley Dam project, when both it and US 285 were rerouted.
evidence.quote: Utility lines were moved, highways US 285 and NM 137 were rerouted

evidence.claim: The older McMillan Reservoir had been filling with silt, and a 1964 study identified inadequate spillway capacity and a risk of failure at both McMillan and Avalon dams.
evidence.quote: In the 1960s, the McMillan Reservoir was silting up, reducing its storage capacity.

evidence.claim: Congress approved the new project in 1972; dam construction began in 1984, and concrete work finished in autumn 1987.
evidence.quote: Congressional approval for the project was given in 1972

evidence.claim: a 1964 study identified inadequate spillway capacity and a risk of failure at both McMillan and Avalon dams.
evidence.quote: A 1964 study of the McMillan and Avalon Dams concluded: "a potential flood would exceed existing spillway capacity at McMillan Dam and cause the dam to be overtopped, which would cause the failure of both dams."

evidence.claim: dam construction began in 1984, and concrete work finished in autumn 1987.
evidence.quote: In 1984, construction on the dam began.  Concrete work was completed by autumn 1987

evidence.claim: From US 285 north of Carlsbad, NM 137 heads west toward the mountains.
evidence.quote: From US285 north of Carlsbad, turn west onto NM137.

evidence.claim: Sitting Bull Falls is a separate excursion from the highway, with a short path from parking to the falls viewing area.
evidence.quote: There is an ADA accessible path to the falls viewing area a short distance from the parking lot

evidence.claim: Farther exploration along NM 137 reaches Five Points Vista, with views of the Guadalupe Mountains and their western Rim.
evidence.quote: Scenic drives in the district include an approximately 50-mile trip west from Carlsbad on N.M. 137 to 5 Points Vista, a scenic overlook with views of the Guadalupe Mountains and the Rim

evidence.claim: The full state highway continues to the Texas line, becoming Dog Canyon Road as it enters Guadalupe Mountains National Park.
evidence.quote: NM 137's southern terminus is at the Texas–New Mexico state line, where it becomes Dog Canyon Road as it enters Guadalupe Mountains National Park.

evidence.claim: Sitting Bull Falls is a separate excursion from the highway
evidence.quote: From north of Carlsbad, take Highway 137 from US 285, and then follow Forest Road 276.

evidence.claim: Prickly pear and sotol grow in patches among cream-colored limestone outcrops.
evidence.quote: Large patches of prickly pear and sotol grow out of cream-colored limestone outcrops

evidence.claim: Brantley Dam combines a concrete center with earth-fill wings on the Pecos River.
evidence.quote: Brantley Dam has a concrete gravity center section flanked by rolled earth-fill wings to the east and west

evidence.claim: Its construction changed transport routes as well as water storage: US 285 and NM 137 were rerouted, and the Santa Fe Railway was realigned.
evidence.quote: Utility lines were moved, highways US 285 and NM 137 were rerouted, and a $15,000,000 realignment of the Santa Fe Railway was constructed.

evidence.claim: Work on the dam began in 1984.
evidence.quote: In 1984, construction on the dam began.

evidence.claim: After the concrete work finished in autumn 1987, the Pecos was diverted through the new floodgates.
evidence.quote: Concrete work was completed by autumn 1987, and soon after, the Pecos River was diverted through the new Brantley floodgates for the first time.

evidence.claim: The resulting lake serves irrigation and flood control, and part of the dam and surrounding land belongs to Brantley Lake State Park.
evidence.quote: A part of the dam and surrounding land form the Brantley Lake State Park.

evidence.claim: on the Pecos River
evidence.quote: dam on the Pecos River

evidence.claim: The resulting lake serves irrigation and flood control
evidence.quote: Benefits include irrigation, flood control

evidence.claim: Spring water feeds Sitting Bull Falls, dropping 150 feet into a pool below.
evidence.quote: spring-fed waterfalls that fall 150 feet (45.7 m) to a large pool of water below.

evidence.claim: Above the drop, water passes through streams and pools; below it, most disappears into gravel or cracks in the rock.
evidence.quote: The water flows through a series of streams and pools until reaching the falls where it drops 150 feet into the canyon below. Most of the water disappears into the gravel or cracks in the rocks

evidence.claim: It reappears farther down the canyon or joins the Pecos Valley’s underground water supply.
evidence.quote: either reappears in springs further down the canyon or joins the Pecos Valley underground water supply.

evidence.claim: The picnic area includes stone buildings constructed by the Civilian Conservation Corps in 1940.
evidence.quote: In 1940, the Civilian Conservation Corps constructed a number of stone buildings which are part of the parking and picnic area.

evidence.claim: Several shelters were repaired after a wildfire damaged the area in 2011.
evidence.quote: The day use area was closed from April 27, 2011 through April 6, 2012 due to damage from a wildfire in the area. A number of the shelters were repaired after fire had damaged them.

evidence.claim: Notice the CCC stone buildings in the parking and picnic area.
evidence.quote: In 1940, the Civilian Conservation Corps constructed a number of stone buildings which are part of the parking and picnic area.

evidence.claim: The entry gate closes at 3:30 p.m.; the site closes at 4 p.m. Day use only, with no overnight camping.
evidence.quote: The site is open seven days a week, from 8:30 a.m. - 4:00 p.m. Entry gate is closed by 3:30 p.m.

evidence.claim: Day use only, with no overnight camping.
evidence.quote: Day use only. No overnight camping permitted.

evidence.claim: Five Points Vista overlooks the Guadalupe Mountains and the Rim, a cliff 1,500 to 2,000 feet high along the range’s western edge.
evidence.quote: 5 Points Vista, a scenic overlook with views of the Guadalupe Mountains and the Rim, the 1500' - 2000' cliff that extends the entire north–south length of the district and which marks the western edge of the Guadalupe range.

evidence.claim: The trip west from Carlsbad along NM 137 is approximately 50 miles.
evidence.quote: an approximately 50-mile trip west from Carlsbad on N.M. 137 to 5 Points Vista

evidence.claim: The surrounding Guadalupe Ranger District forms the back reef of the northern Capitan Reef.
evidence.quote: the Guadalupe Ranger District forms the back reef of the northernmost section of the Capitan Reef.

evidence.claim: That Permian reef partly enclosed the Delaware Sea.
evidence.quote: the Capitan Reef, a Permian period (299 to 251 million years ago) barrier that partially encircled the Delaware Sea

evidence.claim: The district changes from steep-walled southern canyons to rolling hills and smaller canyons draining east toward the Pecos valley.
evidence.quote: a series of steeply walled canyons before gradually changing into rolling hills and small canyons that run east into the valley of the Pecos River.

evidence.claim: The Rim marks the western edge of the Guadalupe range.
evidence.quote: the Rim, the 1500' - 2000' cliff that extends the entire north–south length of the district and which marks the western edge of the Guadalupe range.

evidence.claim: The Guadalupe Ranger District occupies an exposed part of the Capitan Reef, a Permian barrier that partly enclosed the Delaware Sea.
evidence.quote: The district is part of the Guadalupe Mountain range, an exposed area of the Capitan Reef, a Permian period (299 to 251 million years ago) barrier that partially encircled the Delaware Sea

evidence.claim: The concrete spillway has six radial gates; earth-fill wings extend to either side of the central structure.
evidence.quote: The concrete section has a central overflow spillway controlled by six radial gates

evidence.claim: A short accessible path leads from the parking lot to the viewing area, with additional hiking trails in the recreation area.
evidence.quote: There is an ADA accessible path to the falls viewing area a short distance from the parking lot, along with several hiking trails.

evidence.claim: The Guadalupe area became part of Lincoln National Forest in 1917, when the Alamo National Forest was dissolved.
evidence.quote: When the Alamo was disestablished in June 1917, the Guadalupe area became part of the Lincoln National Forest

flags: Cache supports tourism promotion as a scenic byway, but not the BLM designation, 1994 date, State Scenic Backway status or precise 28.7-mile mapped endpoint. Full NM 137 and Five Points excursion are not presented as the mapped byway length.

Dropped current claim that Five Points is well past the mapped endpoint: cache lacks that endpoint. Dropped 200-foot waterfall implication: tourism describes a 200-foot tufa wall, while Forest Service and waterfall article give a 150-foot drop. Used manager’s drop measurement.

Forest Service page has differing road references: introductory directions use Forest Road 276, detailed directions use County Road 409. Turn-by-turn excursion instructions omitted pending reconciliation.

Retained Sitting Bull coordinates exactly as required, although Forest Service gives a different latitude/longitude. Brantley Dam coordinates come from its Wikipedia COORDINATES line; no dam-top access is promised.
Moments run from the Pecos-side approach into the mountains, using source geography; strip map lacks these excursion points. Five Points has no eligible coordinate source and remains unpinned.
